content: Stamford Hospital is a private, nonprofit community and teaching hospital located in Stamford, Connecticut. It is affiliated with 440 physicians and has a capacity of 305 inpatient beds, which are distributed across various specialties, including medicine, surgery, obstetrics/gynecology, psychiatry, and critical care units for both medical and surgical patients. As of 2005, the hospital employed a total of 2,254 staff members. The Tandet Center, a nursing home previously operated by the hospital and located adjacent to its main building, was recently sold. The center employed 65 workers, while an additional 100 hospital employees are represented by the New England Health Care Employees Union, District 1199, which is affiliated with the Service Employees International Union. Stamford Hospital offers healthcare services to its employees without requiring deductibles if they utilize the hospital's own facilities. The hospital is led by its president, Brian Grissler. In early 2007, Stamford Hospital launched the Familial Colorectal Cancer Registry, a pioneering initiative in Connecticut aimed at individuals and families with a history of colorectal or related cancers. This private registry provides members with general screening information, updates on the latest research, and access to a dedicated website. Awards and Recognition In 2004, the Joint Commission on Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations awarded Stamford Hospital the prestigious Ernest A. Codman Award for its development of a protocol to maintain optimal blood glucose levels in critically ill patients. This protocol resulted in a 29% reduction in mortality rates among these patients and an 11% decrease in their length of stay in the intensive care unit. In 2005, the American Nursing Credentialing Center recognized the hospital for excellence in nursing services, making it one of only 168 hospitals nationwide to receive this honor. Additionally, in 2007, Ernst & Young LLP presented Brian Grissler with the Entrepreneur of the Year award in the social enterprise category. Cardiology Services The hospital's Cardiology Department, which includes 32 beds, expanded its services in August 2005 by introducing emergency angioplasty. By early 2007, the hospital planned to offer open-heart surgery and elective angioplasty. The Richard & Hinda Rosenthal Cardiology Unit, a newly opened 24-bed facility, provides care for more acute cardiac patients in a setting designed to be warmer and more home-like. This unit includes eight specialized beds for patients requiring additional advanced care. Tully Health Center The Daniel P. & Grace I. Tully & Family Health Center, located at 32 Strawberry Hill Avenue, was named in honor of the Tully family, who made a significant donation to the Campaign for Stamford Hospital. Opened in the spring of 2002 on the site of the former St. Joseph's Hospital, the center offers a wide range of services, including diagnostic imaging, ambulatory surgery, the Women's Breast Center, the Heart Institute, the Professional Pharmacy, the Southern Connecticut Vascular Center, the Immediate Care Center, outpatient mental health services, and the Health & Fitness Institute. Other Locations At 26 Palmer's Hill Road, the hospital operates the Rehab Center, the Children's Health Center, adult day services, and Skill Source. In June 2006, the hospital opened the Darien Imaging Center at 6 Thorndal Circle to provide outpatient radiology services. Alliances and Partnerships Stamford Hospital is a major teaching affiliate of Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons, offering training programs in internal medicine, family practice, psychiatry, obstetrics/gynecology, and surgery. The hospital is also a member of the Planetree Alliance, a nationwide group of hospitals dedicated to patient-centered care. History Stamford Hospital was established on May 7, 1896, with an initial capacity of 30 beds in a mansion on East Main Street, west of the railroad bridge. The hospital's founding was made possible by John Clasen, a farmer and former state legislator, who sold some of his property to raise approximately $45,000 for the project. Clasen was inspired to start the hospital by his friend and attorney, Edwin L. Scofield, who later became Stamford's second mayor. Clasen stipulated that the hospital be named Stamford Hospital, remain nonsectarian, and not discriminate in accepting patients. Recent History Between 1994 and 2000, Stamford Hospital experienced financial difficulties, losing money in six of those years, including a $22 million loss in one year. By 2001, the hospital's pension plan was underfunded by $40 million. Brian Grissler became president and CEO in 2001. In response to these challenges, approximately 200 employees were laid off in 2002 and 2003, and the hospital faced declining market share. However, the hospital's financial situation began to improve, with revenues reaching $357 million in 2007. That same year, Ernst & Young LLP recognized Grissler with its Entrepreneur of the Year award in the social enterprise category.
